body: Perhaps the clearest takeaway from Tuesday's US midterms is that data centers are unpopular. After a short-lived construction boom, they provide little ongoing employment and drive up local energy costs. There were 41 local votes on data center curbs and 40 of them are on track to win, with margins in the 75/25% range. Microsoft and Amazon are heavily into the data center business, including huge plans to build more so they should be losers today, right? Wrong. Shares of those two are up around 7% and the market cheers a slower, smaller data center buildout. The market has been hating the massive spending on highly-inflated chips and data center supply chains. In effect, the market is saying that the government is doing for you what you should be doing. Now the companies themselves have been trying to sell Wall Street on data center economics but the cash demands are simply too high and the market has said that the risk-reward isn't convincing. At this point, there might be some reflexivity in company management. Now that they've seen how the stock reacts to data center curbs, they might slow their own ambitions to levels closer to matching free cash flow. If so, that could be a powerful tailwind for the stocks, which have struggled this year. Amazon is particularly compelling as its core business of goods delivery isn't under threat from AI in the same way as a software company like Microsoft. The flipside is that the companies in the data center building business are struggling. The neoclouds and vendors are all down big today, along with the companies that would be contract to provide the power to the data centers. Forthe next moves, watch what kind of agenda congressional Democrats set around AI and data centers. They have a wide menu of things to choose to go after, including rampant corruption. I tend to think that some level of oversight around AI is coming but I'm not sure they want to take on data centers at the national level. Another spot to watch is in Texas and Ohio, where more than one-quarter of planned data center capacity is located. Both of the new Democratic governors campaigned against data centers and it will be critical to see how they plan to act. Most important those are voters, who have clearly showed they don't want to pay higher electricity rates so OpenAI can run the data centers harder. The host country will invite the attending nations to sign onto a voluntary pledge to reach 35 percent electrification on a global level by 2035. Just a year ago, this target may have seemed overly ambitious, but now, experts say that a number of factors, including volatile oil and gas markets stemming from the war in Iran, paired with enormous advances in clean energy technologies, have put that goal within “striking distance.” The months-long closure of the Strait of Hormuz has catalyzed the clean energy transition and the rate of electrification around the world. Before the United States and Israel began their military offensive in Iran back in February of this year, one fifth of the world’s oil and gas trade flowed through the Strait of Hormuz. Its abrupt closure therefore sent global oil and gas markets into turmoil and sent energy-importing countries around the world scrambling for alternatives, especially ones that they could produce and control on their home soil. And, just like that, renewable energy became the new face of energy security . “Wind and solar cannot be embargoed, blockaded, or shut off by a foreign power,” David Frykman, General Partner at Stockholm-based venture capital group Norrsken, wrote in an op-ed for Fortune earlier this year. “Every terawatt-hour of domestic renewable generation is a terawatt-hour that no adversary can weaponize.” But there is another, quieter force that has made this rapid global pivot toward renewable energies possible – the energy storage boom. Energy storage is critical to ensure grid stability in the face of rapid electrification and the increasing representation of intermittent energy sources like wind and solar power in national energy mixes. Major advances in the sector in recent years have made battery storage more affordable and more scalable than ever before – just in time for the world’s most recent bout of ‘ fossilflation .’ “What's really become a game-changer in the past two years is the rapid deployment of large-scale batteries that can hang onto ever larger amounts of power to be used throughout the day to smooth out demand and avoid overtaxing the grid,” Forbes wrote in a Monday report . The second quarter of this year saw the United States’ largest-ever energy storage expansion, at 20.2 gigawatt-hours of additional capacity, according to a report by the Solar Energy Industries Association and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That puts this year’s total additions at 30.8 GWh – and counting. “Although President Trump is no fan of renewable energy or batteries, utility-scale energy storage capacity still nearly doubled to 165 GWh from 88 GWh in the first 18 months of his administration,” the Forbes article goes on to detail. “Grid operators, utilities and data center developers are all buying batteries as fast as they can to meet power demand and improve grid reliability. body: Oil Crashes 9% as Trump and Vance Blame Iran War for Midterm Rout The leading economics blog online covering financial issues, geopolitics and trading. The United Arab Emirates currently operates one crude export pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz and announced earlier this year that it was building a second. A third pipeline is reportedly being planned to further expand crude capacity and reroute energy flows around Hormuz, reducing exposure to Iranian disruption and weakening Tehran's leverage over the critical maritime chokepoint. Bloomberg reported Wednesday morning that Abu Dhabi’s state-owned energy giant, Abu Dhabi National Oil Co., is weighing plans for a third pipeline from the UAE’s western coast to Fujairah on its eastern coast that could supply Asian customers and bypass Hormuz. "Adnoc has been telling some customers in Asia about the pipeline, other people familiar with the matter said. The plans haven’t been finalized and could still change, including the route, a number of the people said," the outlet reported. The new pipeline would build on the UAE's existing pipeline, which has operated since 2012 and stretches 252 miles from Habshan in Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. That pipeline has a capacity of 1.5 million barrels a day, expandable to 1.8 million. Earlier this year, the UAE announced the West-East Pipeline, expected to begin operations in 2027 and double export capacity through Fujairah. Notably, Fujairah sits outside the Hormuz chokepoint, allowing tankers to load crude without entering the Persian Gulf. An ADNOC spokesperson responded to the outlet's request for comment: “We have advised Bloomberg that this report is not accurate and purely speculative.” Beyond the UAE, the biggest story of the year has been other US-allied Gulf countries expanding pipeline routes around Hormuz, including Saudi Arabia , while Kuwait is proposing new pipelines. Taken together, these projects could erode Iran's leverage over Gulf flows, which has also clearly carried into US politics, with a Democratic sweep in the midterms. body: The post-election rally in gold on Wednesday brought buyers to a critical test of trend resistance near the 20-day moving average, potentially setting up a bullish reversal if key resistance levels can be reclaimed. Gold rallied to a six-day high of $4,070 on Wednesday, following the U.S. midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party won a majority in Congress. Key trend resistance was tested near the 20-day moving average, currently near $4,075. That average was the first upside target for gold if buyers took control. The test of resistance at that average adds to its significance, as a sustained reclaim would provide an additional sign of strength. Wednesdayâs high now has greater significance, with a subsequent rally above it potentially providing further confirmation of bullish momentum. Although the session is not quite complete, buyers remain in control at the time of writing, and the top of the dayâs range could be higher by the close. The ability to maintain that control into the close will therefore be important. Nevertheless, the test of resistance near the downtrend line also occurred during Wednesdayâs session, and the high was close to the recent interim lower swing high of $4,082. That price area marked a key support zone that held for 10 days during the recent decline and a rally above it would provide a bullish reversal signal for the decline. However, the prior consolidation range that generated support also places the March spike low of $4,098 nearby, adding to the initial resistance zone. Consequently, a sustained advance through this area would represent a more meaningful improvement in the short-term technical picture. An alternative scenario is that Wednesdayâs strength proves unsustainable, at least initially, and sellers regain control before a rally above $4,098 occurs. If support is then found above the 20-day average during a pullback, the potential for further upside may be validated. There is also a higher resistance level near $4,155, established by three lower daily highs during the recent decline. A recovery of that level would further confirm strength during an advance toward the lower swing high of $4,217 from October. That higher level is a key component of the decline that followed the August high, and its recovery would trigger a more significant bullish reversal signal. Thus, the progression from reclaiming $4,082 to overcoming $4,155 and eventually $4,217 provides a series of increasingly important confirmation levels. While K33 Research analysts retain their bullish stance on the Crypto King, they see the potential for a volatility shock in either direction. They therefore prefer strategies based on volatility rather than directional bets. A slight bearish bias towards BTC persists among investors as institutional demand weakens further this week. According to SoSoValue data, Tuesday's modest $115.56 million outflow from BTC spot ETFs followed withdrawals of $398.62 million on Monday. These consecutive sessions of outflows point to continued caution ahead of the US midterm election results. Should withdrawals persist and gather pace through the week, BTC could face a deeper correction. This week's US midterm elections were highlighted as a key driver of market volatility in a report published by K33 Research on Tuesday. Since then, Democrats have gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. This paves the way for a divided government and possible political gridlock over the rest of US President Donald Trump's term, which K33 Research regards as the most market-friendly outcome. According to the report, a substantial change in K33's proprietary regime indicator has been driven by diverging positioning in Bitcoin's Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) futures and perpetual (perp) futures. Comparisons with earlier regimes point to greater BTC volatility but no clear directional bias: past episodes have delivered steep drawdowns as well as sizeable rallies. If the advance extends to that level, earlier supply is likely to return. How The AI Stock Selloff Is Hurting Copper Price - BeInCrypto
body: Copper prices plunged to a three-month low this week as fears over the AI boom spread from technology stocks into commodities. On Tuesday, copper fell 3.2% to $13,883 per ton on the London Metal Exchange. Prices recovered on Wednesday, climbing back above $14,100 following the US midterm elections . The metal has now retreated from its September record of $14,875, raising questions about whether its historic rally is losing momentum. First, the recent AI stock market rout has shaken confidence in the spending boom behind new data centers. Copper is essential for electrical infrastructure, making it a popular investment tied to AI expansion. Marex analyst Ed Meir said copper appeared to be “catching up” with the recent semiconductor selloff. Second, Democrats’ victory in both chambers of Congress has reduced expectations of US tariffs on refined copper. Those tariff fears previously encouraged traders to stockpile copper in America, squeezing supplies elsewhere and pushing prices higher. Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen warned that reduced tariff expectations could hurt copper prices. The surprising development is that physical copper demand remains relatively strong. China’s Yangshan copper premium, a measure of demand for imported metal, remains near $200 per ton, its highest in more than a decade. Meanwhile, Chinese warehouse inventories have fallen more than 75% in six months. Investors are selling copper over economic uncertainty while physical buyers continue competing for limited supplies. On the daily copper chart , prices remain in a descending channel after breaking their upward trendline. The $6.31-per-pound area is critical support, near July’s low. A daily close below it could open the door toward $6.11 and potentially $5.91. A sustained rebound would bring resistance around $6.70 back into focus. Despite the short-term weakness, J.P. Morgan forecasts copper averaging $14,800 per ton in the fourth quarter, supported by supply constraints. The next test is whether China’s demand can outweigh weakening confidence in AI investment. title: AMD Stock Surges 7% as AI Data Center Revenue Jumps 97% to $8.55 Billion - Coinpaper
body: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock surged approximately 7.3% in premarket trading on November 4 after the chipmaker reported record quarterly earnings, with its data-center business nearly doubling as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure accelerated. According to AMD's November 3 earnings release , data-center revenue climbed 97% year over year to $8.55 billion, exceeding Wall Street's $8.20 billion estimate. Total company revenue reached $13.38 billion, increasing 45% from a year earlier. The results mark a significant turnaround from the recent semiconductor selloff , which pushed the Nasdaq-100 into correction territory as investors questioned escalating AI infrastructure costs. AMD reported adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share, ahead of analysts' $1.95 estimate, while adjusted net income climbed 77% to $3.47 billion. Data-center revenue accounted for approximately 64% of total quarterly sales, compared with around 47% a year earlier. Growth was driven by AMD's EPYC server processors and Instinct MI450 AI accelerators, reflecting demand for both traditional computing and AI workloads. The performance strengthens the argument behind earlier AMD stock forecasts , which emphasized that demand for server CPUs could expand alongside GPU-intensive AI infrastructure. AMD also issued fourth-quarter revenue guidance of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, exceeding analysts' $16.23 billion consensus. That would represent roughly 27% sequential growth and 66% annual growth at the midpoint. AMD's stronger results suggest that AI spending is spreading beyond Nvidia's dominant accelerator business. CEO Lisa Su said the company expects overall revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027, above analysts' projected 77% increase, according to Reuters. The company's Helios rack-scale computing systems combine Instinct GPUs with EPYC processors, positioning AMD to compete for larger AI infrastructure contracts. AMD identified Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle among organizations running workloads on its early Helios systems. The expansion comes as investors increasingly question whether enormous capital commitments can generate sustainable returns. An earlier AI market analysis identified more than $2 trillion in technology valuations at risk during October's selloff. Meanwhile, Marvell and Palantir shares recently declined despite substantial AI-related business developments, highlighting the sector's sensitivity to valuation concerns. AMD's earnings offer a different signal: infrastructure demand remains strong even as stock-market enthusiasm becomes more selective. AMD shares have gained approximately 126% in 2026, according to Reuters, leaving investors to assess whether earnings growth can support further valuation expansion. At the reported 7.3% premarket gain, AMD stood to add roughly $58 billion in market capitalization if the advance held. However, the company faces challenges beyond Nvidia's competition. A global memory shortage could constrain AI system production, while its client and gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.72 billion. AMD also reported a $1.1 billion noncash charge related to customer warrants, contributing to a difference between GAAP earnings of $1.46 per share and adjusted earnings of $2.09. Those risks follow a period when AI stocks underperformed the broader market , despite continued growth in corporate AI spending. AMD's earlier earnings-driven rally demonstrated how strongly investors can respond when revenue exceeds expectations. body: A stronger trade surplus is modestly supportive for the Australian dollar, reinforcing the currency’s link to commodity prices. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. The data are unlikely to shift Reserve Bank of Australia expectations on their own, given the volatile gold component. Traders will look to upcoming volume data for a cleaner read on how much net exports are adding to growth. Gas and metals did the heavy lifting for Australia’s trade surplus in September, with a big drop in gold imports doing the rest. Australia’s goods trade surplus widened sharply in September to its largest in seven months, as a rise in exports of liquefied natural gas and metals coincided with a steep fall in gold imports, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday. The surplus on goods trade came in at about A$2.8 billion (around US$2 billion), up from A$184 million in August and well ahead of forecasts for a surplus of roughly A$1 billion or less. Exports rose 2.3% from the previous month, following a 3.7% gain in August. The increase was driven by other mineral fuels, a category that includes liquefied natural gas, and by metals, highlighting the support Australia’s resource sector continues to draw from global commodity demand. Imports fell 3.3%, reversing a 5.8% rise in August. The decline was led by gold, where imports dropped by nearly 35%. Gold flows can be volatile from month to month and often swing the headline balance, so the scale of the drop flatters the underlying improvement to some degree. The figures also suggest the recent rebound in fuel prices has yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill. As a large importer of refined fuel, Australia’s import costs would be expected to rise if higher prices persist, which could narrow the surplus in coming months. At the same time, higher energy prices tend to cut both ways for Australia. As a major exporter of liquefied natural gas and coal, the country benefits from elevated global energy prices on the export side, partly offsetting the cost of more expensive fuel imports. The stronger trade position is a positive for the economy’s external accounts, though its contribution to growth will depend on how the volume of trade, rather than its value, develops over the quarter. Attention now turns to whether commodity export strength can be sustained, and how quickly rising fuel costs feed into imports. Both will shape whether September proves a high point for the surplus or the start of a firmer trend. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: The data offer something for both sides of the BoJ debate: historically sharp cost pressures support further tightening, while slowing hiring and weaker confidence give the cautious camp ammunition. On balance, the release is unlikely to shift December pricing materially, leaving the yen more sensitive to the BoJ minutes and oil-driven inflation signals. Firms citing inflation as a drag on confidence underlines how energy costs from the Middle East are feeding into Japanese business sentiment. Weak export orders point to limited support from overseas demand. Japan’s service providers are still growing and still paying up, but they’re hiring less and feeling gloomier about it. Japan’s services sector grew at a slightly faster pace in October, but a slowdown in manufacturing pulled overall private sector growth to a five-month low, while still-sharp cost pressures kept inflation in focus for the Bank of Japan, according to S&P Global’s latest survey. The S&P Global Japan Services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September, marking a fifth straight month of expansion. Firms said stronger inflows of new work and efforts to broaden their customer base lifted activity, though growth remained modest and below the average so far this year. New orders also picked up slightly, driven by firmer domestic demand. Export business fell again, although the decline was the smallest in six months. Hiring was the weak spot. Services employment rose only marginally, the slowest pace in the current 14-month run of job creation, as some firms reported staff leaving through resignations and retirements. With capacity stretched, backlogs of work increased again. Price pressures slowed but stayed elevated. Input cost inflation fell to an eight-month low and output charges also rose more slowly, yet both remained well above their long-run averages. Business confidence about the year ahead dropped to its weakest since March, with firms citing inflation, an ageing population and labour shortages. The broader picture was softer. The composite PMI, which combines services and manufacturing, slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, its lowest since May, though it still pointed to a 19th consecutive month of growth. Faster services growth was offset by a slower rise in factory output. Across the private sector, job creation slowed to a one-year low and confidence fell to a three-month low. Input costs rose at a historically sharp rate, while growth in prices charged eased to a four-month low. S&P Global said input costs and selling prices, while rising more slowly, were still increasing at a pace that suggests official consumer inflation could stay elevated in the coming months. It added that whether growth loses further momentum and whether cost pressures ease will be key considerations for the BoJ as it weighs further tightening, warning that persistent inflation weighed on confidence and could also constrain demand and hiring. The data arrive on the same day as minutes from the BoJ’s September meeting, which showed policymakers agreed on the need for further rate increases, keeping attention on whether the central bank moves again in December. body: Tuesday's $115.56 million in modest net outflows from spot Bitcoin Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) reflects institutional caution ahead of the US midterm election results. On Wednesday, Bitcoin (BTC) is trading between its key 100-day and 200-day Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs). This price behaviour points to consolidation, with a move beyond either boundary likely to establish BTC's next directional bias. Despite maintaining a bullish view on the Crypto King, K33 Research analysts see scope for a volatility shock in either direction. They therefore favour strategies based on volatility over outright directional positions. SoSoValue figures show that BTC spot ETFs registered modest outflows of $115.56 million on Tuesday, following Monday's $398.62 million withdrawal. Institutional demand has thus continued to soften this week. These successive daily withdrawals indicate that investors are exercising caution ahead of the US midterm election results, while retaining a mildly bearish stance on BTC. A continuation and acceleration of outflows over the rest of the week could lead to a deeper correction in Bitcoin. In its Tuesday report, K33 Research highlighted the US midterm elections as a key driver of market volatility this week. Since then, Democrats have gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. This creates the prospect of divided government and potential political deadlock for the rest of US President Donald Trump's term, which K33 Research regards as the most market-friendly outcome. According to the report, a substantial shift in K33's proprietary regime indicator has been driven by diverging positioning in Bitcoin's Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) futures and perpetual (perp) futures. Comparisons with past regimes point to increased BTC volatility but no clear directional signal: earlier episodes have featured steep drawdowns as well as strong rallies. The analyst added: “While we remain bullish on BTC and believe the bottom is in, thin support and elevated leverage leave room for further downside and amplified liquidation-driven moves,” With three-month implied volatility also close to historically low levels, K33 favours taking positions in volatility rather than choosing a direction. In particular, it favours long straddles, which could benefit from sizeable post-election moves in Bitcoin's price. At the time of writing on Wednesday, Bitcoin stands at $77,876, with price consolidating between the 100-day and 200-day EMAs. The 50-day EMA at $80,044 continues to cap BTC's upside, reinforcing the prospect of further consolidation. On the daily chart, a Relative Strength Index (RSI) reading close to 40 points to muted bullish momentum. The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) histogram is also still below zero. Failure to secure a close above the 100-day EMA, however, could prolong the correction towards initial support at the 200-day EMA, near $76,479.
